title: Shared site failures reduced median linear discrimination in models of eight partial worm maps
abstract: We tested if shared failures at polyadic chemical sites help linear readouts to distinguish input cells. Eight public worm brain maps supplied site membership. We used 110 target cells and 31 input cells that passed the same coverage rule in all maps. Each map gave 465 input pairs. The reference had the same target means and variances but independent contact events. At full sharing and added target noise equal to 0.1 times site variance, median optimal squared discrimination ratios were 0.887 to 0.933. Thus all eight medians fell below the reference. In contrast, 10.3 to 23.4 percent of pairs improved. Readouts fitted to the independent reference gave lower median ratios of 0.777 to 0.857 when tested with shared noise. The median loss remained with raw count signals, partial sharing, and four noise levels. These are local linear model scores, not measured information or behavior. Unknown release coupling, selected cells, partial brain coverage and the lack of activity data limit the result. Code, aggregate results, checks, source hashes and a separate retrieval recipe support reproduction.

display.caption: Median squared linear discrimination against a reference with the same target variances. Left: optimal weights at four added-noise levels. Right: weights fitted to shared noise or to independent noise, at added-noise factor 0.1. Each point describes 465 dependent input pairs in one map. Map order is developmental order; no age trend or animal uncertainty is inferred.

citations.reason: Primary site-level chemical maps from eight worms.
Established dependence of population information on the alignment of signal and noise; no new general information theorem is claimed.
Prior study of nonnegative averaging under shared site failure. Here signed linear readouts distinguish input identities with common background noise; no files or tables reused.
Prior noise-dimension calculation. The present study tests signal-dependent linear discrimination instead of effective noise dimension.
